text: Think not so much of what thou hast not as of what thou hast: but of the things which thou hast select the best, and then reflect how eagerly they would have been sought, if thou hadst them not.
plain: Count what you have by imagining you had lost it.

text: Retire into thyself.
plain: Go inward. Peace is built there, not out in the crowd.

text: Wipe out the imagination. Stop the pulling of the strings. Confine thyself to the present.
plain: Stop the stories in your head. Stay in what is actually happening.

text: About fame: look at the minds [of those who seek fame], observe what they are, and what kind of things they avoid, and what kind of things they pursue. And consider that as the heaps of sand piled on one another hide the former sands; so in life the events which go before are soon covered by those which come after.
plain: Fame is sand piling over sand. What you did today gets buried fast.

text: From Antisthenes: It is royal to do good and to be abused.
plain: Doing right and getting attacked for it is noble, not a loss.

text: Life must be reaped like the ripe ears of corn. One man is born; another dies.
plain: Life gets cut down like grain, and the next one starts.

text: Look round at the courses of the stars, as if thou wert going along with them; and constantly consider the changes of the elements into one another, for such thoughts purge away the filth of the terrene life.
plain: Think about the stars and constant change and the petty stuff drops away.

text: Consider the past,--such great changes of political supremacies; thou mayest foresee also the things which will be.
plain: History repeats. Read the past and you can see what is coming.

text: Everywhere and at all times it is in thy power piously to acquiesce in thy present condition, and to behave, justly to those who are about thee, and to exert thy skill upon thy present thoughts, that nothing shall steal into them without being well examined.
plain: You can always accept where you are, treat people right, and watch what gets into your head.

text: Consider thyself to be dead, and to have completed thy life up to the present time; and live according to nature the remainder which is allowed thee.
plain: Pretend your old life is over and live what is left on purpose.

text: Love that only which happens to thee and is spun with the thread of thy destiny. For what is more suitable?
plain: Love what is happening to you. It is your life.

text: In everything which happens keep before thy eyes those to whom the same things happened, and how they were vexed, and treated them as strange things, and found fault with them: and now where are they? Nowhere.
plain: People before you cried about the same things, and they are gone. Why do it too?

text: Look within. Within is the fountain of good, and it will ever bubble up, if thou wilt ever dig.
plain: The good stuff is inside you. You just have to keep digging.

text: The art of life is more like the wrestler's art than the dancer's, in respect of this, that it should stand ready and firm to meet onsets which are sudden and unexpected.
plain: Life is wrestling, not dancing. Be ready for the hit you did not see coming.

text: When then thou art discontented about any of these things, say to thyself that thou art yielding to pain.
plain: If you are whining about something minor, that is you giving in to pain.

text: Always bear this in mind; and another thing too, that very little indeed is necessary for living a happy life.
plain: You need very little to live happy.

text: It is in thy power to live free from all compulsion in the greatest tranquillity of mind, even if all the world cry out against thee as much as they choose, and even if wild beasts tear in pieces the members of this kneaded matter which has grown around thee.
plain: You can stay calm even if the whole world screams at you.

text: The perfection of moral character consists in this, in passing every day as the last, and in being neither violently excited nor torpid nor playing the hypocrite.
plain: Perfect character is treating every day as your last without panic, laziness or faking.

text: It is a ridiculous thing for a man not to fly from his own badness, which is indeed possible, but to fly from other men's badness, which is impossible.
plain: Run from your own flaws, which you can fix, not from other people's, which you cannot.

text: When thou hast done a good act and another has received it, why dost thou still look for a third thing besides these, as fools do, either to have the reputation of having done a good act or to obtain a return?
plain: Do the good thing and stop. Do not wait for credit or payback.

text: On the occasion of every act ask thyself, How is this with respect to me? Shall I repent of it? A little time and I am dead, and all is gone.
plain: Before you act, ask if you will regret it. You are about to be dead anyway.

text: [Consider] that men will do the same things nevertheless, even though thou shouldst burst.
plain: People will keep doing what they do, no matter how much you rage.

text: This is the chief thing: Be not perturbed, for all things are according to the nature of the universal; and in a little time thou wilt be nobody and nowhere, like Hadrianus and Augustus.
plain: Stay calm. Even emperors end up nobody.

text: All things are change, yet we need not fear anything new.
plain: Everything changes, so nothing new has to scare you.

text: Thou hast not leisure [or ability] to read. But thou hast leisure [or ability] to check arrogance: thou hast leisure to be superior to pleasure and pain: thou hast leisure to be superior to love of fame, and not to be vexed at stupid and ungrateful people, nay even to care for them.
plain: You have no time to read, but you do have time to drop arrogance, beat pleasure and pain, and not get rattled by ungrateful people.

text: When thou risest from sleep with reluctance, remember that it is according to thy constitution and according to human nature to perform social acts, but sleeping is common also to irrational animals.
plain: Dragging out of bed? Humans are made for work. Sleeping in is what animals do.

text: Remember that as it is a shame to be surprised if the fig-tree produces figs, so it is to be surprised if the world produces such and such things of which it is productive; and for the physician and the helmsman it is a shame to be surprised if a man has a fever, or if the wind is unfavorable.
plain: Do not act shocked when the world acts like the world.

text: Remember that to change thy opinion and to follow him who corrects thy error is as consistent with freedom as it is to persist in thy error.
plain: Changing your mind when corrected is freedom, not weakness.

text: Short lived are both the praiser and the praised, and the rememberer and the remembered: and all this in a nook of this part of the world; and not even here do all agree, no, not any one with himself: and the whole earth too is a point.
plain: The praiser and the praised both vanish, and the whole earth is a dot.

text: Thou sufferest this justly: for thou choosest rather to become good to-morrow than to be good to-day.
plain: You suffer because you keep putting off being good until tomorrow.

text: Lucilla saw Verus die, and then Lucilla died. Secunda saw Maximus die, and then Secunda died.
plain: Everyone buries someone, then gets buried.

text: Some indeed have not been remembered even for a short time, and others have become the heroes of fables, and again others have disappeared even from fables.
plain: Some are forgotten fast, some become legend, some are forgotten even by the legends.

text: Pain is either an evil to the body--then let the body say what it thinks of it--or to the soul; but it is in the power of the soul to maintain its own serenity and tranquillity, and not to think that pain is an evil.
plain: The body can feel pain, but your mind decides whether it is an evil.

text: Wipe out thy imaginations by often saying to thyself: Now it is in my power to let no badness be in this soul, nor desire, nor any perturbation at all; but looking at all things I see what is their nature, and I use each according to its value.
plain: Tell yourself you can keep your mind clean of desire and panic, and see each thing for what it is worth.

text: Receive [wealth or prosperity] without arrogance; and be ready to let it go.
plain: Take success without arrogance and be ready to lose it.

text: Do not disturb thyself by thinking of the whole of thy life. Let not thy thoughts at once embrace all the various troubles which thou mayest expect to befall thee: but on every occasion ask thyself, What is there in this which is intolerable and past bearing? for thou wilt be ashamed to confess.
plain: Do not carry your whole life at once. Ask what is actually unbearable right now and it is usually nothing.

text: All this is foul smell and blood in a bag.
plain: Strip off the glamor and the body is just blood in a bag.

text: If thou takest away thy opinion about that which appears to give thee pain, thou thyself standest in perfect security.
plain: Drop your opinion about what hurts you and you are safe.

text: See that thou secure this present time to thyself: for those who rather pursue posthumous fame do not consider that the men of after time will be exactly such as these whom they cannot bear now; and both are mortal.
plain: Live now. People who chase a legacy forget the future crowd will be just as annoying as today's.

text: Take me and cast me where thou wilt; for there I shall keep my divine part tranquil, that is, content, if it can feel and act comformably to its proper constitution.
plain: Put me anywhere and I can stay calm.

text: If then there happens to each thing both what is usual and natural, why shouldst thou complain? For the common nature brings nothing which may not be borne by thee.
plain: Whatever happens is normal for a person, so quit complaining. You can bear it.

text: If thou art pained by any external thing, it is not this thing that disturbs thee, but thy own judgment about it. And it is in thy power to wipe out this judgment now.
plain: It is not the thing, it is your judgment of it. You can drop the judgment now.

text: And even if thou art pained because thou art not doing some particular thing which seems to thee to be right, why dost thou not rather act than complain?
plain: If you are upset about something undone, why not just do it instead of complaining?

text: Remember that the ruling faculty is invincible, when self-collected it is satisfied with itself, if it does nothing which it does not choose to do, even if it resist from mere obstinacy.
plain: Your mind cannot be forced if you refuse to be forced.

text: Say nothing more to thyself than what the first appearances report. Suppose that it has been reported to thee that a certain person speaks ill of thee. This has been reported; but that thou hast been injured, that has not been reported.
plain: Stick to the facts. Someone talked trash about you; you were not injured.

text: A cucumber is bitter--Throw it away.--There are briers in the road--Turn aside from them.--This is enough.
plain: Bitter cucumber, throw it away. Thorns on the road, step around. That is all.

text: Neither in thy actions be sluggish nor in thy conversation without method, nor wandering in thy thoughts, nor let there be in thy soul inward contention nor external effusion, nor in life be so busy as to have no leisure.
plain: Do not be lazy, scattered, or so busy you have no room to breathe.

text: Suppose that men kill thee, cut thee in pieces, curse thee. What then can these things do to prevent thy mind from remaining pure, wise, sober, just?
plain: Even if they ruin you, they cannot touch your character.

text: Dost thou wish to be praised by a man who curses himself thrice every hour? wouldst thou wish to please a man who does not please himself?
plain: Why want praise from people who do not even like themselves?

text: Generally, wickedness does no harm at all to the universe; and particularly the wickedness [of one man] does no harm to another. It is only harmful to him who has it in his power to be released from it as soon as he shall choose.
plain: Other people's badness only hurts the one who keeps it, and they can drop it any time.

text: He who fears death either fears the loss of sensation or a different kind of sensation. But if thou shalt have no sensation, neither wilt thou feel any harm; and if thou shalt acquire another kind of sensation, thou wilt be a different kind of living being and thou wilt not cease to live.
plain: Death is either no feeling or a new kind of feeling. Neither is harm.

text: Men exist for the sake of one another. Teach them then, or bear with them.
plain: Teach people or put up with them. Those are the choices.

text: Do not despise death, but be well content with it, since this too is one of those things which nature wills.
plain: Do not hate death. It is just nature doing its thing.

text: He who does wrong does wrong against himself. He who acts unjustly acts unjustly to himself, because he makes himself bad.
plain: Doing wrong hurts the wrongdoer first.

text: Thy present opinion founded on understanding, and thy present conduct directed to social good, and thy present disposition of contentment with everything which happens--that is enough.
plain: A clear mind, useful acts and peace with what happens is enough.

text: Wipe out imagination; check desire: extinguish appetite: keep the ruling faculty in its own power.
plain: Kill the fantasies, rein in wanting, keep control of your mind.

text: Labor not as one who is wretched, nor yet as one who would be pitied or admired; but direct thy will to one thing only--to put thyself in motion and to check thyself, as the social reason requires.
plain: Work without self pity or showing off. Pick one thing and go.

text: To-day I have got out of all trouble, or rather I have cast out all trouble, for it was not outside, but within and in my opinions.
plain: The trouble was never outside. It was in how I saw things.

text: Everything now is just as it was in the time of those whom we have buried.
plain: Nothing is new. It was the same for everyone already dead.

text: Not in passivity but in activity lie the evil and the good of the rational social animal, just as his virtue and his vice lie not in passivity but in activity.
plain: Good and bad lie in what you do, not in what happens to you.

text: Penetrate inwards into men's leading principles, and thou wilt see what judges thou art afraid of, and what kind of judges they are of themselves.
plain: Look at who you fear to be judged by. See how they judge themselves.

text: All things are changing: and thou thyself art in continuous mutation and in a manner in continuous destruction, and the whole universe too.
plain: You and everything else are always changing.

text: Thou hast endured infinite troubles through not being contented with thy ruling faculty when it does the things which it is constituted by nature to do.
plain: Most of your suffering came from not being at peace with your own mind.

text: When another blames thee or hates thee, or when men say about thee anything injurious, approach their poor souls, penetrate within, and see what kind of men they are.
plain: When someone hates you, look at what kind of person they are.

text: Thou wilt discover that there is no reason to take any trouble that these men may have this or that opinion about thee.
plain: You will find no reason to care what they think of you.

text: Soon will the earth cover us all: then the earth, too, will change, and the things also which result from change will continue to change forever, and these again forever.
plain: Soon the earth covers all of us, and then it changes too.

text: The universal cause is like a winter torrent: it carries everything along with it.
plain: Time is a flood that carries everything away.

text: Set thyself in motion, if it is in thy power, and do not look about thee to see if any one will observe it; nor yet expect Plato's Republic: but be content if the smallest thing goes on well, and consider such an event to be no small matter.
plain: Start moving. Do not wait for anyone to notice. Be glad when even small things go right.

text: Simple and modest is the work of philosophy.
plain: The real work is plain and humble.

text: Look down from above on the countless herds of men and their countless solemnities, and the infinitely varied voyagings in storms and calms, and the differences among those who are born, who live together, and die.
plain: Zoom out. Look at all the people, all the voyages, all the dying. Your problem shrinks.

text: All that thou seest will quickly perish, and those who have been spectators of its dissolution will very soon perish too. And he who dies at the extremest old age will be brought into the same condition with him who died prematurely.
plain: Everything you see will end, and the old and the young die the same.

text: When they think that they do harm by their blame or good by their praise, what an idea!
plain: They think their praise or blame matters. What a thought.

text: Loss is nothing else than change.
plain: Loss is just change.

text: Enough of this wretched life and murmuring and apish tricks. Why art thou disturbed? What is there new in this?
plain: Enough whining. What about this is actually new?

text: If a man has done wrong the harm is his own. But perhaps he has not done wrong.
plain: If someone wronged you, the harm is theirs. Maybe they did not even wrong you.

text: Well, then, is it not better to use what is in thy power like a free man than to desire in a slavish and abject way what is not in thy power?
plain: Be free about what you control. Do not grovel over what you do not.

text: When thou art offended with any man's shameless conduct, immediately ask thyself, Is it possible, then, that shameless men should not be in the world? It is not possible. Do not, then, require what is impossible.
plain: Of course shameless people exist. Do not demand the impossible.

text: Consider whether thou shouldst not rather blame thyself, because thou didst not expect such a man to err in such a way.
plain: Maybe blame yourself for not expecting it.

text: For what more dost thou want when thou hast done a man a service? art thou not content that thou hast done something conformable to thy nature, and dost thou seek to be paid for it?
plain: You did a good thing. Why do you need a payment?

text: Remember, however, that thou art formed by nature to bear everything, with respect to which it depends on thy own opinion to make it endurable and tolerable, by thinking that it is either thy interest or thy duty to do this.
plain: You were built to bear whatever you can see as useful or as your duty.

text: What need is there of suspicious fear, since it is in thy power to inquire what ought to be done?
plain: Why be afraid when you can just figure out what to do?

text: He who follows reason in all things is both tranquil and active at the same time, and also cheerful and collected.
plain: Follow reason and you are calm, active and cheerful together.

text: To her who gives and takes back all, to nature, the man who is instructed and modest says, Give what thou wilt; take back what thou wilt.
plain: Tell nature: give what you want, take what you want.

text: Short is the little which remains to thee of life. Live as on a mountain.
plain: Little time is left. Live like you are on a mountain, above the noise.

text: No longer talk at all about the kind of man that a good man ought to be, but be such.
plain: Stop describing a good man. Be one.

text: Consider what men are when they are eating, sleeping, generating, easing themselves, and so forth. Then what kind of men they are when they are imperious and arrogant, or angry and scolding from their elevated place.
plain: The powerful eat, sleep and use the toilet like you. Remember that when they posture.

text: He then who fears or is grieved or is angry is a runaway.
plain: Fear, grief and anger are all running away from reality.

text: Imagine every man who is grieved at anything or discontented to be like a pig which is sacrificed and kicks and screams.
plain: Complaining about what cannot change is a pig squealing on the way to the altar.

text: When thou art offended at any man's fault, forthwith turn to thyself and reflect in what like manner thou dost err thyself; for example, in thinking that money is a good thing, or pleasure, or a bit of reputation, and the like.
plain: When someone's fault bothers you, look at your own, like treating money or reputation as the real good.

text: Let it not be in any man's power to say truly of thee that thou are not simple or that thou art not good; but let him be a liar whoever shall think anything of this kind about thee; and this is altogether in thy power.
plain: Do not let anyone truthfully say you are not good. That is up to you.

text: But a brief existence is common to all things, and yet thou avoidest and pursuest all things as if they would be eternal.
plain: Everything is brief and you chase and flee it like it will last forever.

text: A little time, and thou shalt close thy eyes; and him who has attended thee to thy grave another soon will lament.
plain: Soon your eyes close, and the one who buried you gets buried too.

text: The healthy eye ought to see all visible things and not to say, I wish for green things; for this is the condition of a diseased eye.
plain: A healthy eye takes whatever it sees. Demanding only the pleasant is the sickness.

text: There is no man so fortunate that there shall not be by him when he is dying some who are pleased with what is going to happen.
plain: Even the best person has people glad to see them go. Do not take it personally.

text: In all things, then, except virtue and the acts of virtue, remember to apply thyself to their several parts, and by this division to come to value them little: and apply this rule also to thy whole life.
plain: Break pleasures into parts and they shrink. Only virtue holds up.

text: Have I done something for the general interest? Well then, I have had my reward. Let this always be present to thy mind, and never stop [doing such good].
plain: If you did something useful, that is the reward. Keep going.

text: Let then thy judgment about them be at rest, and they will remain quiet, and thou wilt not be seen either pursuing or avoiding.
plain: Calm your judgment about the things you chase and flee, and they go quiet.

text: Suppose any man shall despise me. Let him look to that himself. But I will look to this, that I be not discovered doing or saying anything deserving of contempt.
plain: Let them despise me. I will make sure I do nothing that deserves it.

text: Such as a man's character is, he immediately shows it in his eyes, just as he who is beloved forthwith reads everything in the eyes of lovers.
plain: Your character shows in your eyes. You cannot hide it.

text: Nothing is more disgraceful than a wolfish friendship [false friendship]. Avoid this most of all.
plain: Fake friendship is the worst. Stay away from it.

text: Take away these opinions then, and resolve to dismiss thy judgment about an act as if it were something grievous, and thy anger is gone.
plain: Drop the judgment about what they did and the anger goes.

text: For he who yields to pain and he who yields to anger, both are wounded and both submit.
plain: Yielding to pain and yielding to anger are both losing.

text: He who has not one and always the same object in life, cannot be one and the same all through his life.
plain: If you have no single aim, you are a different person every day.

text: The Pythagoreans bid us in the morning look to the heavens that we may be reminded of those bodies which continually do the same things and in the same manner perform their work, and also be reminded of their purity and nudity. For there is no veil over a star.
plain: Look at the sky every morning. Stars do the same work every night with nothing to hide.

text: Neither in writing nor in reading wilt thou be able to lay down rules for others before thou shalt have first learned to obey rules thyself. Much more is this so in life.
plain: You cannot give rules before you can follow them.

text: All those things at which thou wishest to arrive by a circuitous road thou canst have now, if thou dost not refuse them to thyself.
plain: What you want at the end of the long road you can have now if you stop refusing it.

text: I have often wondered how it is that every man loves himself more than all the rest of men, but yet sets less value on his own opinion of himself than on the opinion of others.
plain: We love ourselves most but trust our own opinion of ourselves less than anyone else's.

text: Practise thyself even in the things which thou despairest of accomplishing. For even the left hand, which is ineffectual for all other things for want of practice, holds the bridle more vigorously than the right hand; for it has been practised in this.
plain: Practice what you think you cannot do. Your weak hand gets strong from practice.

text: Consider in what condition both in body and soul a man should be when he is overtaken by death; and consider the shortness of life, the boundless abyss of time past and future, the feebleness of all matter.
plain: Think about how you want to be found by death and how short and fragile it all is.

text: In the application of thy principles thou must be like the pancratiast, not like the gladiator; for the gladiator lets fall the sword which he uses and is killed; but the other always has his hand, and needs to do nothing else than use it.
plain: Be a pancratiast, not a gladiator: keep your hand and never drop the weapon.

text: And even if the tempest carry thee away, let it carry away the poor flesh, the poor breath, everything else; for the intelligence at least it will not carry away.
plain: The storm can take your body. It cannot take your mind.

text: Does the light of the lamp shine without losing its splendor until it is extinguished? and shall the truth which is in thee and justice and temperance be extinguished [before thy death]?
plain: The lamp shines until it goes out. Truth and justice in you should too.

text: If it is not right, do not do it: if it is not true, do not say it.
plain: If it is wrong, do not do it. If it is false, do not say it.

text: Perceive at last that thou hast in thee something better and more divine than the things which cause the various affects, and as it were pull thee by the strings.
plain: There is something in you better than whatever pulls your strings.

text: Consider that before long thou wilt be nobody and nowhere, nor will any of the things exist which thou now seest, nor any of those who are now living.
plain: You will soon be nobody, nowhere, and so will everyone you know.

text: Consider that everything is opinion, and opinion is in thy power. Take away then, when thou choosest, thy opinion, and like a mariner who has doubled the promontory, thou wilt find calm, everything stable, and a waveless bay.
plain: Everything is opinion, and you control your opinion. Drop it and the sea goes calm.

text: Cast away opinion: thou art saved. Who then hinders thee from casting it away?
plain: Drop the opinion and you are saved. Who is stopping you?

text: Smoke and ash and a tale, or not even a tale.
plain: It all ends as smoke and ash, and maybe a story.

text: What remains, except to enjoy life by joining one good thing to another so as not to leave even the smallest intervals between?
plain: Enjoy life by stacking good things with no gaps.

text: How small a part of the boundless and unfathomable time is assigned to every man, for it is very soon swallowed up in the eternal!
plain: Your share of time is tiny and gets swallowed up fast.

text: Reflecting on all this, consider nothing to be great, except to act as thy nature leads thee, and to endure that which the common nature brings.
plain: Nothing is great except acting from your nature and enduring what comes.

text: Depart then satisfied, for he also who releases thee is satisfied.
plain: Leave content, because the one who lets you go is content too.
